episode_title: What Are You Selling And What's It Worth? - Self Storage Fundamentals Part 3

real_qa.q: What is value pricing in self-storage and how do hotel and airline industries demonstrate this concept?
real_qa.r: Value pricing is knowing the value of the empty space surrounded by metal walls that you rent, recognizing that not all space is worth the same amount. Hotels and airlines exemplify this through tiered options: airlines offer main cabin with limited legroom, main select with extra legroom, and premium with complimentary drinks. Hotels similarly advertise different room types at different price points—a tiny one-bed room at $189 versus a larger room at $213—allowing customers to choose the amenities that justify the price difference.
real_qa.requete: value pricing self-storage hotel airline model

real_qa.q: How should self-storage operators handle odd-sized units like 10 by 11 or 9 by 10 to avoid customer confusion?
real_qa.r: Operators should lump several different sizes into standard categories like the 10 by 10 price tier. For example, a true 10 by 10 might be priced at $100, a 9 by 10 at $95 (marked as having less legroom), and a 10 by 11 at $110 (as a premium variant with extra square footage). This keeps the menu from getting cluttered with 15 different sizes while still accommodating unit variations. Clearly mark the actual dimensions on listings so customers understand what they're renting.

real_qa.q: What terminology should self-storage facilities use to describe unit types to match customer search behavior?
real_qa.r: Facilities should stick to terms customers actually search for: use either 'standard,' 'drive up,' 'standard indoor,' or 'standard hallway access' for non-climate-controlled units. For climate-controlled units, stay consistent with what local competitors call them—if all competitors use 'temperature controlled,' align with that terminology. Define these terms clearly in the lease, as 'climate controlled' doesn't mean you're actually controlling the climate; it describes what the unit provides.

real_qa.q: How does occupancy rate influence pricing strategy in self-storage facilities?
real_qa.r: Pricing depends on whether a facility is in lease-up or stabilized status. If stabilized at 90-95% or higher occupancy, 90 percent of the pricing weight comes from occupancy level—you can set rates aggressively because you're full. If sitting at 75-80% occupancy and needing bodies in units, you may need to discount, but avoid driving prices down indiscriminately because you'll look back six months later at low revenue and struggle to pull rates back up.

real_qa.q: What is the tiered pricing strategy (value, standard, premium) and how does showing a crossed-out price increase perceived value?
real_qa.r: Tiered pricing presents three unit options: value at $90, standard at $100 (shown as normally $125 marked down), and premium at $135. The customer perceives the standard unit as a bargain—they think it's regularly $125 but getting it for $100, only $10 away from premium but $35 cheaper. This psychological pricing nudges customers toward the middle tier and the $100 target rather than settling for the $90 option, increasing perceived value.
